title: At the control-room door
objectives: Build a five-minute tumbling summary with an outcome threshold.
Recognize bucket-boundary effects and threshold limitations.
Follow up with a focused success-action search and check chronology manually.
Distinguish Search output from detection rules and verified incident conclusions.
story: MIDNIGHT AT MERIDIAN / CHAPTER 6 — The sponsor finally admits the VIP slide came in a demonstration package. A backstage checklist also exposes a shared publishing password. That explains a risky path, but who used it and when are still open questions. Check short failure bursts and prepare a focused successful-login follow-up. Finish with a defensible handoff, not a convenient culprit.

teaching.heading: Check capability before using windows
teaching.text: Google documents these tumbling windows as preview/pre-GA, with availability depending on customer and region. Do not enable a preview for this course. Missing capability leaves workplace practice pending.

teaching.heading: A bucket has an edge
teaching.text: by 5m makes fixed five-minute groups, not every possible rolling five-minute period. Activity across a boundary can split into separate groups.

teaching.heading: A threshold is a filter, not a verdict
teaching.text: condition: $failures > 3 keeps summary groups above three. Four records can meet that teaching threshold; they do not prove four attacks or authorize an operational detection.

teaching.heading: Follow up and keep chronology private
teaching.text: A second ALLOW search for an account can support a follow-up. Compare times and identity context inside SecOps. Two independent queries alone do not prove that success followed failure or shared a session.

teaching.heading: A useful handoff separates facts from hypotheses
teaching.text: State the observed change, relevant account/host/time scope, competing explanations and next evidence needed. Failure bursts followed by success can matter, but these separate queries do not establish a sequence or who was behind an account. Do not turn a teaching threshold into a detection standard.

challenges.title: Put failures into five-minute buckets
challenges.prompt: Select USER_LOGIN, FAIL action, and nonempty principal.user.userid. Group by that user in fixed five-minute buckets. Output distinct metadata.id count, retain count > 3, order descending by that count, and limit to 20 rows.
challenges.referenceQuery:
metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
security_result.action = "FAIL"
principal.user.userid != ""
$user = principal.user.userid
match:
  $user by 5m
outcome:
  $failures = count_distinct(metadata.id)
condition:
  $failures > 3
order:
  $failures desc
limit:
  20
acceptedVariants:
events:
  principal.user.userid != ""
  security_result.action = "FAIL"
  metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
match:
  principal.user.userid by 5m
outcome:
  $n = count_distinct(metadata.id)
condition:
  $n >= 4
order:
  $n desc
limit:
  20
hints: Extend the earlier grouped distinct-record summary with a five-minute tumbling bucket.
Use by 5m in match and compare the outcome count in condition; keep order and limit.

methodQuestions.prompt: Why can a short burst be split into two lower counts?

options.label: order desc divides large groups into equal halves.
Its events can fall on opposite sides of a fixed bucket boundary.
limit 20 divides the input time range into twenty buckets.

methodQuestions.rationale: Fixed five-minute buckets have boundaries; one short sequence can span two of them.

methodQuestions.prompt: Which integer-count condition is equivalent to $failures > 3?
methodQuestions.rationale: > 3 retains counts 4, 5, 6 and higher. >= 4 does the same; = 4 would exclude higher counts.

mission.beat: Could failures be clustered into a short burst rather than spread across rehearsal? Build five-minute buckets and use the supplied teaching threshold. This is a Search summary, not a deployed detection rule.

explanation.meaning: A group for each account in fixed five-minute buckets.
A name for the distinct-record count in each group.
Keep groups with at least four counted records.
Rank those summaries, then show up to twenty.

mission.remember: A bucket has edges. A threshold is not a verdict.
mission.caseUpdate: Case clue: a failure burst would justify a timing follow-up. It would not, by itself, prove password spraying, a successful compromise or which person used the account.
mission.caveat: Google documents tumbling windows as preview/pre-GA and customer/region dependent. Do not enable a preview for this course. If unavailable, continue with the course example.

analystNote.text: A burst can come from retries or automation. Password spraying usually concerns attempts across accounts; this account-grouped query alone cannot establish it. Bucket boundaries can split a burst.

challenges.title: Build the final follow-up yourself
challenges.prompt: Select USER_LOGIN events with ALLOW action and principal.user.userid exactly [USER]. Return event rows. This query alone does not establish success-after-failure chronology.
hints: Choose the candidate user inside SecOps; keep only [USER] on the site.
Use USER_LOGIN, ALLOW action, and the exact actor userid as required filters.

methodQuestions.prompt: Does this separate ALLOW search prove those events occurred after the earlier failures?

options.label: Yes; running the ALLOW query second establishes event order.
Yes; the USER_LOGIN type links each success to its previous failure.
No; the filters do not join the searches or enforce their time order.

methodQuestions.rationale: Query execution order is not event chronology. A separate filter does not express a cross-event time relationship.

methodQuestions.prompt: Which version preserves the requested successful-login account scope?

options.label: USER_LOGIN OR ALLOW OR the exact principal account.
USER_LOGIN AND ALLOW AND the exact principal account.
USER_LOGIN AND (ALLOW OR the exact principal account).

methodQuestions.rationale: All three requirements must hold together. The alternatives admit records that fail at least one required condition.

mission.beat: Mira needs one precise follow-up: allowed login records for the principal publishing account. Write it from memory. Compare chronology only in SecOps; the course needs your query, not the evidence.

explanation.meaning: Ask for the recorded allowed action.
Keep the exact symbolic actor account in scope.

mission.remember: A good final query answers a precise question and knows its limits.
mission.caseUpdate: CASE HANDOFF — The unapproved VIP slide came with the sponsor's demo package; a shared password left the publishing path poorly controlled. Your queries scoped access, roles, process and network leads. The intern is not proven responsible, and the operator remains unconfirmed. Hand off the evidence gaps instead of inventing a culprit.
mission.caveat: This query alone does not establish success-after-failure. Compare chronology and identity context only in workplace tools.

analystNote.text: An allowed-login query does not prove success-after-failure. Keep account/host context and event times together when following up privately. A good handoff states what is supported and what evidence is still missing.
